lesson.title: Isotopes: Same Element, Different Weight
lesson.summary: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that share an atomic number but differ in neutron count and therefore in mass number.
lesson.body:
Not every atom of a given element weighs exactly the same, and isotopes are the reason why. An isotope is defined as one of two or more forms of the same element whose atoms have the same atomic number, meaning the same number of protons, but different mass numbers, meaning different numbers of neutrons. Because atomic number fixes element identity, isotopes of the same element are chemically almost identical: they bond the same way, react in the same reactions, and occupy the same square on the periodic table. What differs is purely nuclear, the neutron count, and consequently the atom's mass and, in some cases, its nuclear stability.

Isotopes are named by writing the element name followed by the mass number, such as carbon-12, carbon-13, and carbon-14, all of which have atomic number 6 and therefore six protons, but differ in neutron count: six, seven, and eight neutrons respectively. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are both stable and occur naturally, making up about 98.9 percent and 1.1 percent of natural carbon respectively, while carbon-14 is radioactive and occurs only in trace amounts, formed continuously in the upper atmosphere and used for radiocarbon dating of once-living material.

The same pattern shows up throughout the periodic table. Chlorine has two major naturally occurring isotopes: chlorine-35, with 17 protons and 18 neutrons, and chlorine-37, with 17 protons and 20 neutrons. Both are stable, both behave identically in chemical reactions such as forming table salt with sodium, and both are found mixed together in every natural sample of chlorine gas or chloride compounds, roughly three parts chlorine-35 to one part chlorine-37. This mixing of isotopes in fixed natural proportions is what eventually leads to the concept of average atomic mass, since the mass value listed on the periodic table for chlorine, 35.45, reflects this blend rather than either isotope alone.

A worked example ties isotopes directly back to atomic number and mass number. Boron has atomic number 5. One natural isotope, boron-10, has a mass number of 10, giving it 10 minus 5, or 5 neutrons. The other major natural isotope, boron-11, has a mass number of 11, giving it 11 minus 5, or 6 neutrons. Both isotopes have exactly 5 protons, so both are boron, but boron-11 carries one extra neutron compared to boron-10. Naturally occurring boron is a mix of roughly 20 percent boron-10 and 80 percent boron-11, and that specific mixture is what a mass spectrometer can measure directly.

Isotopes matter far beyond bookkeeping. Some isotopes, like carbon-14 or uranium-238, are unstable and undergo radioactive decay, releasing energy over time as their nuclei rearrange toward more stable configurations. Others, like carbon-12 and chlorine-35, are perfectly stable and simply exist as a normal part of an element's natural composition. Either way, understanding isotopes as atoms sharing atomic number but differing in neutron count is what makes it possible to explain why elements have the specific, often non-whole-number masses listed on the periodic table.
